title: Design Underground System
description: Brute force to optimized: storing every completed trip and rescanning per query versus maintaining a running sum and count per route.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Design an underground railway system that tracks customer travel times between stations. Implement checkIn(id, stationName, t) (record a customer starting a trip), checkOut(id, stationName, t) (record a customer ending a trip that they checked into), and getAverageTime(startStation, endStation) (return the average time it has taken customers to travel between these two specific stations, across every completed trip on that route).

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Track an in-progress event, then finalize it later\"","A hash map from id to the in-progress event's start info, cleared once finalized"],["\"Running average over an accumulating group of records\"","Maintain a running sum and count per group, rather than storing every individual record"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Each customer's trip has two separate events (checkIn and checkOut) that must be correlated by their id to compute the trip's duration. Once a trip completes, only its CONTRIBUTION to that specific route's average time matters going forward, not the individual trip record itself.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Turnstile Log Correlated by Ticket Number
blocks.text: Picture a turnstile system where tapping in records your ticket number, station, and time, and tapping out at another station looks up that same ticket number to compute how long the trip took. Once computed, that duration just gets folded into a running total and count for that specific station-to-station route, not kept as an individual record forever.

blocks.caption: One map correlates in-progress trips by id; another maintains running totals per completed route

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: several checkIn/checkOut pairs, then getAverageTime queries
Results: 14.00000, 11.00000, null, null, 12.00000 for the getAverageTime calls, computed from the running sum/count maintained per route as trips complete.
5. How Should We Think?

Before storing every individual completed trip and scanning them all when getAverageTime is called, notice that only the SUM of travel times and the COUNT of trips for a given route are ever needed to compute an average, so maintaining a running sum and count per route directly (updated incrementally on each checkOut) avoids any scanning at query time.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: checkIn and checkOut for the same customer must be correlated by their id, so a map from id to (station, time) at check-in time is needed to compute the trip's duration once checkOut arrives.

Observation 2: Once a trip's duration is computed at checkOut time, it only ever needs to be FOLDED into a running total, since averages can be maintained incrementally without keeping every individual data point.

Observation 3: A second map, keyed by the (startStation, endStation) route, storing a running (total time, trip count) pair, lets checkOut update this in O(1), and getAverageTime simply divide totalTime by count in O(1).

Observation 4: The in-progress map entry for a customer's id can be discarded (or simply left to be overwritten by their next trip) once checkOut processes it, since it is no longer needed.

This leads to two hash maps: one from customer id to their in-progress check-in info, and one from route (start, end) to a running (total time, count) pair, updated incrementally so getAverageTime is a direct O(1) division.
6. Brute Force Solution
Store every completed trip as an individual record (start station, end station, duration). For getAverageTime, scan all records matching the requested route and compute the average directly.
Step by step algorithm

items: On checkIn, record the customer's starting station and time in a map keyed by id.
On checkOut, look up the starting info by id, compute the duration, and append a full trip record (start, end, duration) to a growing list.
On getAverageTime, scan the ENTIRE list of trip records, summing durations for matching (start, end) routes and dividing by their count.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Storing every completed trip individually preserves full historical detail, which is more than the problem ever asks for.
getAverageTime must rescan the ENTIRE trip history every time it is called, which is wasteful when only the aggregate sum and count are ever needed.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) for checkIn/checkOut, O(total trips) per getAverageTime call.
Space: O(total trips).
Limitation: maintaining a running sum and count per route directly, updated at checkOut time, makes getAverageTime an O(1) division instead of an O(total trips) scan.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why storing every individual trip is unnecessary: getAverageTime only ever needs the SUM of durations and the COUNT of trips for a specific route, never the individual trip details.

The incremental aggregation trick: maintain a second map keyed by the route (startStation, endStation), storing a running (totalTime, count) pair; on every checkOut, look up this pair for the relevant route, add the new trip's duration to totalTime, and increment count.

Why this preserves correctness: since averages are just totalTime divided by count, maintaining these two running aggregates incrementally, rather than storing individual data points, produces the exact same result at query time, just computed once per checkOut instead of rescanned per query.

The core idea: two hash maps, one correlating in-progress check-ins by id, one maintaining running (sum, count) aggregates per route.

Maintain a map from id to in-progress check-in info, and a map from route (start, end) to a running (totalTime, count) pair. checkOut computes the duration and updates the route's running pair directly. getAverageTime looks up the pair and divides in O(1).

Dry run for a Leyton -> Waterloo route with two completed trips

blocks.caption: Running (totalTime, count) per route makes getAverageTime an O(1) division

blocks.text: Why This Works

Since an average is fully determined by just a sum and a count, maintaining these two aggregates incrementally as each trip completes produces mathematically identical results to storing and later summing every individual trip, but without ever needing to rescan history. The id-keyed map correctly correlates each checkOut with its matching checkIn, since ids are guaranteed to check in before checking out in valid usage.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) for checkIn, checkOut, and getAverageTime.
Space: O(active check-ins + distinct routes).
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Design Underground System is a clean example of the "maintain running aggregates instead of storing raw history" technique, whenever only a summary statistic (like an average) is ever queried, not individual records.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to remove or overwrite the id-keyed check-in entry after checkOut, though this is often harmless since a new checkIn for the same id would overwrite it anyway.
Recomputing the average by re-scanning stored trips instead of maintaining a running sum and count, missing the intended optimization.

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly stating "only a running sum and count are needed for an average, not the full history" shows recognition of a broadly reusable aggregation technique.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "maintain a running average over an accumulating set of events", think: a running sum and count per group, updated incrementally, avoiding any rescanning.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you support removing or correcting a previously recorded trip?
How would you extend this to report the median trip time instead of the average?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Any "maintain a running average/statistic over an accumulating stream of events" design problem.
Two-map correlation designs generally, pairing an in-progress-event map with an aggregated-results map.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Storing every trip and scanning for getAverageTime costs O(total trips) per query; maintaining running (sum, count) aggregates per route costs O(1) for every operation, the standard efficient design.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: maintain running aggregates (sum and count) per group, rather than storing and rescanning raw individual records.
Core Idea: correlate checkIn/checkOut by customer id; on checkOut, fold the trip's duration into a running (totalTime, count) pair for that specific route.
Time: O(total trips) per getAverageTime query for the brute force, O(1) for all operations in the optimized approach.
Space: O(total trips) versus O(active check-ins + distinct routes).
Most Important Observation: an average only ever needs a sum and a count, never the full history of individual values.
Interview Difficulty: an accessible, practical design problem about choosing the right aggregate representation.
One line memory trick: two maps: id to in-progress trip, route to running (sum, count).
